tr.td: Daniel Morcombe, 13, who was waiting for a bus to Sunshine Plaza
Guilty of murder, indecent treatment of a child under 16 and interfering with a corpse, Queensland Supreme Court, 13 March 2014
Life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 20 years, imposed by Justice Roslyn Atkinson on 14 March 2014
The conviction appeal was dismissed in May 2015; a separate appeal by the former attorney-general, Jarrod Bleijie, to lengthen the non-parole period was also rejected
Brett Peter Cowan, 44 at the time of the verdict and a father of three, according to the Examiner
Angus Edwards, who argued at sentencing that his client had not intended to kill Daniel, according to the Canberra Times
Six men and six women; a unanimous verdict on all three charges
"Almost eight hours", according to the Canberra Times
Three and a half years for indecent treatment and two years for interfering with a corpse, served concurrently, according to The New Daily
Seventeen bones and two sandshoes found at a sand mining site off Kings Road, Glass House Mountains; clothing found in Coochin Creek nearby
Two for sexual offences against young boys; the Canberra Times reported offences against boys, committed in Brisbane and Darwin in 1987 and 1993, and the jury was not told of the convictions

content.p: Brett Peter Cowan was a man with two earlier convictions for sexual offences against young boys when he was tried in Brisbane for the abduction and killing of Daniel Morcombe, a 13-year-old who vanished from a bus stop on the Sunshine Coast on 7 December 2003. A jury of six men and six women found him guilty of murder in March 2014, more than ten years after the boy disappeared. The case drew the largest police investigation in Queensland's history, and it was solved by an undercover operation that produced a recorded confession and, in the end, the boy's remains.
content.h2: The bus stop under the overpass
content.p: Daniel lived in Palmwoods with his parents, Bruce and Denise Morcombe, and his twin brother, Bradley. According to the prosecution's account set out in the 2013 ruling of the Supreme Court, Daniel told his brothers after lunch that he planned a trip to Sunshine Plaza for a haircut and some Christmas shopping. He left home before 2 p.m. and walked about 1.3 kilometres to a bus stop on Nambour Connection Road. The prosecution also said that Daniel and his twin brother took that bus to the plaza about every four or five weeks. Daniel waited on the northern side of the Kiel Mountain Road overpass, at what the court described as an unofficial stop.

The first scheduled bus broke down about 750 metres short of the overpass, and a replacement bus was sent through as an express service. As it passed under the overpass at about 2.15 p.m., the driver and several witnesses saw Daniel hailing it. The driver signalled that a second bus was following, which would pick him up. Witnesses also saw a man standing some distance behind the boy. The shuttle bus following went through about three minutes later, at about 2.18 p.m., and by then Daniel had gone.

When the boy did not come home, his parents, who had arrived back at about 4.30 p.m., first asked the bus company and later that day reported him missing. Witnesses had described a blue sedan in the area that Sunday, and one described a white four-wheel-drive near the overpass. The investigation that followed became, according to the Examiner, the largest police investigation in Queensland's history.

Cowan became a suspect within two weeks of the disappearance, according to the Examiner. Police examined his white Mitsubishi Pajero for fingerprints and blood, but found nothing incriminating, and the lead went cold. Other people confessed to the killing over the period, but, as the Examiner put it, none of them led police to the boy's remains.

The turn came in 2011, when Cowan was arrested after a covert police operation. A commentary republished by the Bond University research portal says that a covert method known as the Mr Big technique led to the arrest, although police made no direct public reference to it in the Morcombe case. Undercover operatives took on the identities of criminal gang members, according to the Examiner.

The operation ran for about four months before Cowan led police to the remains, according to the Examiner. He took the officers to a macadamia farm and then to an abandoned sand pit on Kings Road, in the Glass House Mountains. Next he showed them a bridge spanning Coochin Creek, saying he had tossed Daniel's clothing from it. Seventeen bones and the boy's two sandshoes were eventually recovered from the sand mining site. Shorts and the elastic band of underwear were found in the creek, metres from the bridge.

The prosecutor, Michael Byrne QC, asked the jury how a man could find the right spot among many sand mining sites on the Sunshine Coast. "And yet, he not only got the right sand mining site, he got the right bridge," Byrne told the jury, according to the Examiner. He argued that Cowan could only have known where the body and clothes were from his own part in events, because "he killed Daniel, he dumped his body, he threw away his clothing."

In the 2013 ruling, the court recorded that Cowan had indicated he would admit at trial that skeletal remains whose DNA was consistent with Daniel's had been found during a search of the Kings Road site, together with shoes, and that remnants of clothing had been found in the creek bed nearby. The court also recorded the prosecution's case that Cowan offered to drive the boy to Maroochydore, took him instead to a demountable building on Kings Road, indecently dealt with him, killed him, disposed of the body nearby. Those were allegations, and the jury had to decide them.

Before the trial, Cowan's lawyers asked the court to exclude everything he had said to police, including what the judgment calls admissions by word or conduct. The admissions had been obtained through the undercover operation. For that application he conceded that the admissions could not be called unreliable, and he argued that they had not been made voluntarily, or that they should be excluded in the court's discretion because they were unfair. The court refused the application, and the statements went to the jury.

The court also ruled on evidence of Cowan's earlier offending. The judgment records that he had two prior convictions for sexual offences against young boys. The Canberra Times reported that he had served nine years in jail for offences against boys, committed in Brisbane and Darwin in 1987 and 1993. The jury did not hear about those convictions, a point the Canberra Times noted when it reported the sentencing.

The verdict came from the Queensland Supreme Court, and Cowan was 44 when the jury returned. The six men and six women found him guilty of all three charges: murder, indecently dealing with a child under 16, and improperly dealing with a corpse. The Canberra Times reported that the jury deliberated for almost eight hours before reaching a unanimous decision. Daniel's parents sat in the public gallery each day of the trial, listening to the evidence about their son's final moments. His twin brother, Bradley, and his eldest brother, Dean, were also in the gallery.

On 14 March 2014 Justice Atkinson sentenced Cowan to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 20 years. The prosecution had argued for a longer period than the 15-year minimum, and the Canberra Times reported that the prosecutor cited Cowan's earlier convictions, including the rape of boys aged six and seven. The defence argued for leniency on the ground that he had not meant to kill the boy.

In her remarks, the judge said Cowan had shown "no remorse" and was "beyond rehabilitation", but she left the question of his release to the parole board, The New Daily reported. She told him: "You didn't look like a monster, you didn't look like a paedophile, you looked like an ordinary person." Daniel's parents were not in court for the sentence. With Cowan in the courtroom, Denise Morcombe described him, in a victim impact statement, as a "perverted soul" who had underestimated the family's drive to catch her son's killer, the Canberra Times reported. Hetty Johnston, the founder of the child-protection group Bravehearts, felt the term fell short of what she wanted, while accepting it was the best the system could offer.

Cowan's lawyers appealed on six grounds. Among them were concerns about prejudicial media coverage during the trial and the claim that police had improperly obtained his confession. In May 2015 the Queensland Court of Appeal upheld the jury's verdict. The former attorney-general, Jarrod Bleijie, had separately asked the court to increase the 20-year non-parole period as manifestly inadequate, and that bid was also rejected. Cowan's lawyer, Tim Meehan, said his client had been realistic about his prospects and that police had "overstepped the mark" in the investigation.

In June 2015 Cowan's lawyers lodged an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court. SBS reported that Denise Morcombe had learned of it from the television news and had not been advised. She wrote on Twitter: "Why is the family of Daniel not advised? Don't we count?" Bruce Morcombe was in court in May 2015 when the appeal was dismissed. Outside court, he said: "Today we hope that Mr Cowan doesn't forget his actions," according to The New Daily.

Queensland's premier at the time, Campbell Newman, said the undercover officers should be rewarded. He praised the officers who ran the undercover operation and thanked the family for setting up the Daniel Morcombe Foundation to teach children about predators. The police commissioner, Ian Stewart, was more guarded. He said that the more widely undercover methods became known, the less effective they were, and he was unhappy that such methods had to be aired before a jury to secure a conviction.

The case began with a boy who had no body and no crime scene, and it was solved eight years after he vanished. The Examiner described the wait for justice as "a long time coming" for the Morcombe family. Daniel was laid to rest on 7 December 2012, nine years after he disappeared, at a service attended by hundreds on the Sunshine Coast. The bus stop where he waited was an unofficial one under the Kiel Mountain Road overpass, and the court's own account of that afternoon, with its broken-down bus and the second bus that was following, is the record that remains of how he was last seen.
